title: Castel Sant'Angelo in Rome: what the ticket covers, the terrace, and whether it is worth it
subtitle: A Roman tomb, a fortress, a prison and a papal apartment under one ticket, with a roof that looks straight at St Peter's.
excerpt: What you see inside Castel Sant'Angelo with the standard ticket, what the terrace gives you, who should go and who can skip it, what the Passetto di Borgo is, and what the partner's tickets and audio tours include.
longtail_phrases: is Castel Sant'Angelo worth visiting

meta_title: Castel Sant'Angelo: what the ticket covers, is it worth it
meta_description: What the Castel Sant'Angelo ticket covers, from Hadrian's tomb to the terrace facing St Peter's, how long it takes, and who can skip it.

featured_image.alt: The round drum of Castel Sant'Angelo and the arches of Ponte Sant'Angelo reflected in the Tiber in warm light

content_html:
[place attraction="castel-sant-angelo" city="rome"]

On the morning of 6 May 1527 an unpaid imperial army broke into Rome. Pope Clement VII was in the Vatican palace. He was hurried out along the top of a wall, about eight hundred metres long, that runs from the palace to a round fortress on the Tiber. Most of the Swiss Guard died near St Peter's that morning, holding the attackers back while he ran. The pope reached the fortress, and stayed shut inside it for seven months while the city below was sacked.

The fortress had not been built for popes. It began as a tomb: the emperor Hadrian ordered it for himself and his family, and it was finished in 139, a year after his death. Later it became part of the city wall, then a castle, a prison, a papal apartment and finally a museum. All of those layers are still inside, stacked one above the other, and one ticket takes you up through them to the roof. Whether that is worth two hours of a short stay in Rome depends on what you expect to find.

What the ticket covers

There is one standard ticket, and it covers the whole building. You follow a route that climbs from the Roman tomb to the terrace:

  • The spiral ramp. A Roman corridor under a brick vault, about 125 metres long, that winds up inside the drum of the mausoleum. Hadrian's funeral procession went this way.
  • The Hall of Urns. The chamber at the centre, where the ashes of Hadrian and of the emperors after him, down to Caracalla, were kept. It is bare: the urns were lost long ago.
  • The Courtyard of the Angel, open to the sky, with piles of stone cannonballs and the marble angel by Raffaello da Montelupo that stood on the summit until the eighteenth century.
  • The papal apartments. Rooms painted in the 1540s for Paul III, the largest of them the Sala Paolina, and the strongroom where the papal treasure was kept in iron-bound chests.
  • The loggias and the walkway round the upper drum, with a café along one stretch.
  • The terrace, under the bronze angel.

A wall of the Sala Paolina, the hall painted in the 1540s for Pope Paul III. Photo: Vassil, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.

The terrace

The route ends on the flat roof at the very top. Above you stands the archangel Michael in bronze, made in the 1750s by the Flemish sculptor Peter Anton von Verschaffelt, sliding his sword back into its sheath. He recalls the legend that gave the castle its name: in 590, during a plague, Pope Gregory the Great led a procession past the tomb and saw the archangel on its summit putting away his sword, as a sign that the plague was over.

To the west, the dome of St Peter's rises at the end of a straight avenue. Below, the Tiber bends under Ponte Sant'Angelo, a Roman bridge that Hadrian built to reach his tomb, lined with ten angels carved to Bernini's designs in the late 1660s. To the south and east lie the roofs and domes of the old city. The last act of Puccini's Tosca is set on this roof, and ends with the heroine leaping from its parapet.

In the morning the sun is behind you when you look at St Peter's. Towards evening the dome becomes a silhouette.

From the upper levels: the Tiber, a bastion of the castle, and the dome of St Peter's. Photo: Sonse, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

The bronze archangel above the terrace, putting his sword back in its sheath. Photo: Dennis G. Jarvis, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.

Is it worth it

  • Yes, if you want one high view of Rome. Few others have the dome of St Peter's in them at this distance.
  • Yes, if you like buildings that show their age in layers. You walk from the second century to the sixteenth in half an hour.
  • Yes, with children who like castles. There are ramparts, cannon, a drawbridge and long dark ramps.
  • Less so, if you have two days in Rome and have not yet seen the Forum or the Vatican Museums. Those come first.
  • Less so, if you expect a great art museum. The collections of arms, ceramics and paintings are modest. The building is the exhibit.
  • Think twice if stairs are a problem. The route is made of ramps and many steps, and help for visitors who cannot climb is limited.

The outside costs nothing. The bridge, its angels and the walk round the star-shaped outer walls can be seen at any hour.

The passage to the Vatican

The wall along which Clement VII ran is the Passetto di Borgo, built in 1277 under Pope Nicholas III. It still joins the Vatican to the castle, and you can follow it from the street below or look down on it from the bastions. The corridor itself is visited only on guided tours, booked ahead with a ticket of their own, and the arrangements have changed more than once in recent years. The standard castle ticket does not include it.

The Passetto di Borgo, the walled passage between the Vatican and the castle, seen from outside. Photo: Krzysztof Golik, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

How long, and when

Allow an hour and a half, or two hours with a stop at the café. In season a line forms at the ticket desk from the middle of the morning. A ticket bought in advance saves that line, but everyone passes the same security check. Like other state museums in Italy, the castle has free-entry days, when the line is at its longest. Opening hours and closing days are on our page for Castel Sant'Angelo.

Reading the partner's listings

  • A skip-the-line ticket is entry to the castle. The listing gives no itemised list of what is included. Its description speaks of a coordinator who meets you and takes you to the entrance, after which you visit alone. Check the meeting point and the hour before you pay.
  • A ticket for the castle and the Pantheon is two entries to two places twenty minutes apart on foot. Read how the time for each is set.
  • An entry ticket with an audio tour and a walk adds commentary in the partner's app, on your own phone, for the castle and for a short route round the bridge and the Borgo quarter. The listing excludes the inside of the Passetto, a live guide and earphones.
  • A ticket with a city audio tour pairs entry to the castle with a long audio walk across Rome, as far as the Colosseum. The listing says the commentary for the castle itself comes through a separate app, and that tickets for the other places on the way are not included.
  • An audio walk without a ticket passes the castle from outside, on a route that starts at the Vatican.

These are the tickets and audio tours our partner sells for Castel Sant'Angelo, with today's prices:

[partner q="castel sant angelo" match="castel" limit="5"]

From here

Cross Ponte Sant'Angelo and you are in the lanes that lead, in ten minutes, to Piazza Navona. In the other direction the avenue runs straight to St Peter's Square. See what else there is in Rome, or open the trip planner for Italy.

Cover photo: Jean-Pol Grandmont, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

faqs.q: Is Castel Sant'Angelo worth visiting?
faqs.a: Yes, if you want a high view of Rome with St Peter's in it, or like a building that shows eighteen centuries in layers. If you have only two days and have not seen the Forum or the Vatican Museums, those come first.

faqs.q: What does the Castel Sant'Angelo ticket include?
faqs.a: The standard ticket covers the whole route: the Roman spiral ramp, the Hall of Urns, the Courtyard of the Angel, the papal apartments, the loggias and the terrace. It does not include the Passetto di Borgo.

faqs.q: How long does a visit to Castel Sant'Angelo take?
faqs.a: About an hour and a half, or two hours with a stop at the café on the upper walkway.

faqs.q: Can you go to the top of Castel Sant'Angelo?
faqs.a: Yes. The route ends on the terrace under the bronze angel, with a view of the Tiber, the bridge and the dome of St Peter's. You reach it by ramps and stairs.

faqs.q: Can you walk the Passetto di Borgo?
faqs.a: Only on a guided tour booked ahead, with a separate ticket, and the arrangements change. You can always see the wall from the street and from the bastions of the castle.

title: The Grand Canal by vaporetto: which line to take, which ticket to buy, and what you see from the boat
subtitle: Line 1 from end to end, the side to sit on, the stops worth getting off at, and when a day pass makes sense.
excerpt: How to see the Grand Canal in Venice from the public water bus: line 1 or line 2, a single ticket or a pass, where to board and where to stand, what passes on each bank in order, and what the partner sells.
longtail_phrases: which vaporetto goes down the Grand Canal
is a vaporetto day pass worth it in Venice
which side to sit on the vaporetto on the Grand Canal
how long does vaporetto line 1 take
what can you see from the vaporetto on the Grand Canal
meta_title: Grand Canal by vaporetto: which line, which ticket
meta_description: Line 1 or line 2, single ticket or pass, where to board and stand, and what passes on each bank of the Grand Canal between the station and San Marco.

featured_image.alt: The Grand Canal in Venice seen from the Accademia bridge, with palaces on the left and the domes of Santa Maria della Salute at the far end

content_html:
[place attraction="rialto-bridge" city="venice"]

Venice has no main street. It has the Grand Canal: a reversed S of water, nearly four kilometres long, with around 170 palaces along it, most of them built between the thirteenth and the eighteenth century. The families who built them put the grand front on the water, because that was where guests arrived. The door on the alley behind was the back door. For most of the city's history there was one bridge across, at Rialto. The second came only in 1854.

That is why the canal cannot be seen properly on foot. In 1881 a small steamboat called the Regina Margherita began carrying passengers along it, to the anger of the gondoliers. Its descendants are the vaporetti, the public water buses, and they are still the cheapest way to see the canal from one end to the other. Three things decide how good the trip is: the line, the ticket, and where you stand.

Line 1 or line 2

  • Line 1 is the slow one. It calls at every landing stage on the canal, from Piazzale Roma and the railway station to San Marco, and goes on to the Lido. From the station to San Marco takes about 45 minutes. This is the line to take for the view.
  • Line 2 skips most stops and does the same stretch in about half an hour. It also runs the other way round the city, through the wide Giudecca Canal. At the station, read the board: a line 2 boat that does not say Rialto will get you to San Marco without passing a single palace.

Board at Piazzale Roma if you can, one stop before the station. The boat starts there, so you choose your place.

A vaporetto on the Grand Canal. The open area at the back is the place to stand. Photo: Jean-Pol Grandmont, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.

Which ticket

  • A single ticket is valid for 75 minutes from the moment you validate it. That covers one full run of the canal.
  • A pass for one, two, three or seven days gives unlimited rides on the city's boats, the islands of the lagoon included. Because the single fare is high, a day pass has usually paid for itself by the third ride.

Every ticket is validated by holding it against the reader at the landing stage, each time you board. Inspectors do check.

Two things are easily confused with boat tickets. On some days of the year Venice asks day visitors to book and pay an access fee: it is a separate matter, and whether your date is one of those days is worth checking before you travel. And the gondola ferries that still cross the canal at a few points are paid in cash on board, with no ticket at all.

Where to stand

Some boats have a few open seats at the bow. Most have an open area at the stern. The cabin has low windows and is the worst place for looking. No place shows both banks well, so choose a side:

  • going from the station to San Marco, the left has the Ca' d'Oro and the long run of palaces before Rialto;
  • the right has the market, Ca' Rezzonico, the Guggenheim palace and the Salute.

With a pass, ride it once each way. The boats are fullest between ten and five. Early morning and the hour before sunset give better light and more room.

What passes, in order

From the station towards San Marco:

  • San Simeon Piccolo (right), the church with the green copper dome opposite the station.
  • Ca' Vendramin Calergi (left), a Renaissance palace where Richard Wagner died in 1883. It houses the casino.
  • San Stae and Ca' Pesaro (right): a white church front, then a heavy Baroque palace by Baldassare Longhena, now the city's gallery of modern art.
  • Ca' d'Oro (left), built in the 1420s and 1430s, with the finest Gothic stonework on the canal.
  • The Rialto market (right), busy in the morning, and then the Rialto Bridge: a single stone arch finished in 1591 to replace a line of wooden bridges.
  • The bend. Ca' Foscari, now the university, stands on the corner (right). After it comes Ca' Rezzonico (right), the museum of eighteenth-century Venice, with Palazzo Grassi opposite.
  • The Accademia bridge, with the picture gallery at its foot (right).
  • Palazzo Venier dei Leoni (right), a single white storey that was never built higher. Peggy Guggenheim lived there from 1949 until her death in 1979, and her collection is inside.
  • Santa Maria della Salute (right), the domed church by Longhena that the city vowed during the plague of 1630, and the customs point beyond it.

Then the water opens, and the Doge's Palace and the bell tower of San Marco are in front of you.

The Ca' d'Oro, on the left as you come from the station. The stonework was once gilded. Photo: Ermell, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The Rialto Bridge, for almost three centuries the only way across on foot. Photo: kallerna, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Where to get off

With a pass, the canal becomes a way of visiting. San Stae is the stop for Ca' Pesaro. Rialto Mercato puts you among the fish and vegetable stalls. Accademia is five minutes on foot from the Guggenheim. Salute is at the door of the church, which is free to enter. With a single ticket, stay on board: getting off ends the sightseeing.

Palazzo Venier dei Leoni, never built above its first storey: the Peggy Guggenheim Collection. Photo: Wolfgang Moroder, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

Reading the partner's listings

  • A vaporetto tour with ticket is an audio commentary plus one single boat ticket, valid 75 minutes.
  • An audio tour with a daily pass is the same commentary plus a pass for 24 hours on the public boats.
  • An audio tour for the vaporetto, without more words in its name, is the commentary alone. You buy the boat ticket yourself.
  • With the first two you receive a booking code, not a boat ticket. The listing explains that the code must be exchanged at a ticket machine or a ticket office before you board, and names the stop at the station as the starting point.
  • The commentary is written for line 1, from the station to San Marco. It plays in the partner's app on your own phone. Bring earphones: there is no guide on the boat.
  • Fast track tickets for the Peggy Guggenheim Collection and for Ca' Pesaro are museum entries with no boat ride. Their listings give no itemised list, so check the date and time rules.

These are the Grand Canal audio tours and the tickets for two museums on its banks that our partner sells, with today's prices:

[partner city="venice" match="vaporetto,grand canal,guggenheim,pesaro" limit="5"]

From here

From San Marco the same line 1 carries on to the Lido and its beaches. Line 2 across to San Giorgio Maggiore takes a few minutes, and the bell tower of that church has a lift and a wide view over the city. Our pages for the Rialto Bridge, the Ca' d'Oro and Santa Maria della Salute have current hours. See the rest of Venice, or open the attractions map of Italy.

Cover photo: kallerna, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

faqs.q: Which vaporetto goes down the Grand Canal?
faqs.a: Line 1 stops at every landing stage and takes about 45 minutes from the station to San Marco. Line 2 is faster with fewer stops, but check that the boat goes by way of Rialto.

faqs.q: Is a vaporetto day pass worth it in Venice?
faqs.a: Usually yes if you board three times or more in a day, because the single fare is high. With a pass you can also get off along the canal and ride it once in each direction.

faqs.q: Which side should you sit on the vaporetto on the Grand Canal?
faqs.a: Going from the station to San Marco, the left has the Ca' d'Oro and the palaces before Rialto. The right has the market, Ca' Rezzonico, the Guggenheim palace and the Salute.

faqs.q: How long does vaporetto line 1 take along the Grand Canal?
faqs.a: About 45 minutes from the railway station to San Marco. A single ticket is valid for 75 minutes from validation, which covers it.

faqs.q: Do you need a guide to see the Grand Canal?
faqs.a: No. The public boat passes every palace. An audio commentary on your phone or a list of what stands on each bank is enough to know what you are looking at.

title: Milan Cathedral: which ticket to buy, and whether to take the lift or the stairs to the terraces
subtitle: Five things are sold at the Duomo, alone and combined. What each one is, how long it takes, and how to get onto the roof.
excerpt: The Duomo of Milan sells the cathedral, the museum, the archaeological area and the terraces in several combinations. What each part is, which ticket fits which visitor, lift or stairs to the roof, and what the partner sells.
longtail_phrases: which ticket to buy for the Duomo in Milan
Duomo terraces lift or stairs
how many steps to the Duomo rooftop
is the Duomo archaeological area worth it
how long do you need at Milan Cathedral
meta_title: Milan Duomo tickets: terraces by lift or by stairs
meta_description: Cathedral, museum, archaeological area, terraces by lift or stairs: what each Duomo ticket covers, which one fits your visit, and when to go up.

featured_image.alt: The white marble front and the spires of Milan Cathedral seen from the square under a deep blue sky

content_html:
[place attraction="milan-cathedral" city="milan"]

Work on the cathedral of Milan began in 1386. Gian Galeazzo Visconti, the lord of the city, wanted it in marble and not in the local brick, and he gave the builders a quarry at Candoglia, near Lake Maggiore, about a hundred kilometres away. The blocks came by water: down a river, across the lake, and along a canal to a basin a few hundred metres from the site. The barges were marked AUF, for ad usum fabricae, "for the use of the works", and paid no tolls. Italians still say a ufo for something had for nothing.

The office set up in 1387 to run the works, the Veneranda Fabbrica del Duomo, has never closed. The front was finished only on the orders of Napoleon, who was crowned King of Italy inside in 1805, and the last bronze door was hung in 1965. The Fabbrica still owns the quarry, still replaces worn stones, and sells the tickets. It does not sell one ticket. It sells five things, alone and in combinations, and the names on the screen make sense only when you know what the five are.

The five things

  • The cathedral. Five aisles and 52 pillars, in one of the largest churches in the world. Look for the statue of St Bartholomew flayed, carved by Marco d'Agrate in 1562, who wears his own skin like a cloak, and for the brass line laid across the floor near the entrance in 1786 as a sundial. A small red light high in the vault above the choir marks the place where a nail said to be from the Cross is kept.
  • The terraces. You walk on the roof itself, among 135 spires. On the tallest stands the Madonnina, a gilded copper statue of 1774, about 108 metres above the square.
  • The archaeological area. Under the square, reached from inside the cathedral: the remains of an eight-sided baptistery of the fourth century, where Bishop Ambrose baptised Augustine at Easter in 387.
  • The Duomo Museum, in the Royal Palace next door: original statues and gargoyles brought in from the weather, stained glass seen at eye level, and a wooden model of the cathedral begun in 1519. It is closed one day a week.
  • San Gottardo in Corte, a small palace church of the fourteenth century, entered through the museum.

The nave, between pillars that carry a ring of statues where a capital would be. Photo: Julian Lupyan, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.

Which ticket for whom

  • Cathedral and museum. The basic ticket. Enough if you have an hour, or do not care for heights.
  • The same with the archaeological area. It adds a quarter of an hour underground. Worth it if early Christian history interests you. Otherwise the remains are low walls and a font.
  • Terraces only, by stairs or by lift. For a second visit, or for those who came for the view.
  • A pass for everything, in a stairs version and a lift version. The sensible choice for a first visit with two and a half to three hours.
  • Fast track versions of the pass use a separate line for the lift. They cost more and matter only on the busiest days.

The names of the tickets change from time to time. The five parts do not. People who come to pray use a separate door and need no ticket, but cannot walk round as visitors.

In the Duomo Museum: statues brought in from the weather and replaced by copies outside. Photo: Dimitris Kamaras, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

Under the square: brickwork of the fourth-century baptistery. Photo: Sciking, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Lift or stairs

The stairs are about 250 steps in a narrow stone staircase, enclosed and one-way. A fit adult climbs them in under ten minutes. The ticket is cheaper.

The lift saves that climb, not every step. It brings you out on the lower terraces along the side of the church. From there the route runs under the flying buttresses and then up more flights of steps to the central terrace above the nave. The partner's listings add a warning: the lift is for going up, and the way down is on foot. Neither way is step-free.

In season the lift often has the longer line. If five floors of stairs are no trouble, take the stairs and keep the difference. Choose the lift for bad knees, small children or a hot afternoon.

The central terrace: you walk on the marble slabs of the roof itself. Photo: Daniel Case, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

When to go up

On a clear day after wind or rain, the Alps stand along the northern horizon, with the snow of Monte Rosa to the north-west. In summer the white marble throws back heat and glare at midday and there is no shade: go at opening time or in the last slot of the day. Wet marble is slippery, and the terraces close in storms and frost. Somewhere on the roof there is always scaffolding. Restoration here never ends.

At the door

Everyone passes a security check with a bag scan. Shoulders and knees must be covered, in the cathedral and on the roof alike. Large bags and suitcases are not let in. Rules of this kind are tightened without much notice, so look at our page for Milan Cathedral, which also has the current hours.

Reading the partner's listings

  • The entry ticket is the basic one: the cathedral, and by its description the museum and San Gottardo. No terraces.
  • The entry ticket with archaeological area adds the baptistery under the square.
  • The combo lift ticket lists the cathedral, the museum, the archaeological area and the roof by lift.
  • The ticket with terrace by lift, museum and audio tour gives the same access, with a commentary for the cathedral and the roof in the partner's app.
  • The ticket with audio tour and city walk gives the same access again, and an audio walk that goes on through the Galleria to La Scala, Brera and the new towers of Porta Nuova.
  • The audio tour "without a ticket" is commentary only. Entry is bought separately.

The partner lists no stairs ticket: that one comes from the cathedral's own ticket office. The first two listings give no itemised list of what is included, so read the description before you pay. Audio tours play on your own phone, with your own earphones.

These are the tickets and audio tours our partner sells for the Duomo, with today's prices:

[partner attraction="milan-cathedral" match="duomo" limit="6"]

From here

The glass-roofed Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II opens off the square and is free to walk through. It leads to La Scala in three minutes. Sforza Castle is a quarter of an hour on foot along Via Dante, and its courtyards are free too. See our pages for the Duomo Museum and Sforza Castle, the rest of Milan, or the trip planner for Italy.

Cover photo: Jiuguang Wang, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

faqs.q: Which ticket should you buy for the Duomo in Milan?
faqs.a: For a first visit with two and a half to three hours, a pass that covers the cathedral, the museum, the archaeological area and the terraces. With one hour, the basic ticket for the cathedral and museum.

faqs.q: Should you take the lift or the stairs to the Duomo terraces?
faqs.a: The stairs are about 250 steps and cheaper. The lift saves that climb, but there are still steps from the lower terraces to the central one, and the partner notes that the way down is on foot.

faqs.q: How many steps are there to the Duomo rooftop?
faqs.a: About 250 by the stairs. With the lift you still climb some flights of steps between the lower terraces and the central terrace above the nave.

faqs.q: Is the Duomo archaeological area worth it?
faqs.a: It takes a quarter of an hour and shows the remains of a fourth-century baptistery under the square, where Ambrose baptised Augustine in 387. It is worth it for the history more than for what is left to see.

faqs.q: How long do you need at Milan Cathedral?
faqs.a: About an hour for the cathedral and a look at the museum. Two and a half to three hours for the cathedral, the archaeological area, the museum and the terraces.

title: Verona in a day: the Arena, and what is free or ticketed around it
subtitle: A Roman amphitheatre by day, a loop on foot inside the bend of the river, and a clear idea of which doors to pay at.
excerpt: How to spend one day in Verona: what the Arena visit is, a walking loop from Piazza Bra to Ponte Pietra and Castelvecchio, what is free, what needs a ticket, the truth about Juliet's balcony, and what the partner sells.
longtail_phrases: is one day enough for Verona
can you visit the Verona Arena during the day
what is free to see in Verona

meta_title: Verona in a day: the Arena, what is free, what is ticketed
meta_description: One day in Verona: the Arena by day, a loop on foot to Ponte Pietra and Castelvecchio, what is free, which doors need a ticket, and Juliet's balcony.

featured_image.alt: The two tiers of pink stone arches of the Verona Arena seen from Piazza Bra

content_html:
[place attraction="verona-arena" city="verona"]

The amphitheatre of Verona is about fifty years older than the Colosseum. It was built in the first decades of the first century, outside the walls of the Roman town, and held some thirty thousand people. In 1117 an earthquake brought down almost all of its outer ring. Four arches of that ring are left standing on the north side, and the people of Verona call them the Ala, the wing.

The rest survived because the city never stopped using it, for tournaments, fairs and plays. On 10 August 1913 the tenor Giovanni Zenatello, who was born in Verona, staged Verdi's Aida here for the hundredth anniversary of the composer's birth. The voices carried to the top rows, and opera has come back almost every summer since. So the Arena has two lives, a monument by day and a theatre on summer nights. Around it lies a small Roman and medieval city in a bend of the river Adige, most of which you can see for nothing.

The Arena by day

The visit is simple. You go in under the arches, walk the vaulted corridors that ring the building, and climb the stone tiers, 44 rows of the pink limestone quarried in the hills north of the city, to the rim. There is no museum inside. Half an hour to three quarters is enough.

From June to September the floor is filled with a stage and seats, and pieces of scenery stand stacked on the square outside. On performance days the monument closes to visitors early, often in the afternoon, so in summer go in the morning. An evening at the opera is a different ticket, sold by the festival. The cheapest places are on the Roman steps themselves: take a cushion.

Inside the Arena, with the red seats of the opera season on the floor. Photo: Photo2023, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.

A loop on foot

  • Piazza Bra. The wide square in front of the Arena, with a broad pavement of pink stone along its cafés.
  • Piazza delle Erbe. Ten minutes up the pedestrian Via Mazzini. It was the forum of the Roman town and is still a market, with painted house fronts and a fountain of 1368 that reuses a Roman statue.
  • Piazza dei Signori, through an arch: a quiet square of palaces round a statue of Dante, who spent part of his exile as a guest of the lords of Verona.
  • The Scaliger tombs. Those lords, the della Scala family, are buried beside their church under Gothic stone canopies of the fourteenth century, each topped by a knight on horseback. The tombs stand in the open behind an iron fence, and you see them from the street.
  • Ponte Pietra. The Roman bridge over the Adige. Retreating German troops blew it up in April 1945. It was rebuilt in the 1950s from its own stones, lifted out of the river.
  • Castel San Pietro. Across the bridge, steps climb to a terrace with the classic view of the city inside its loop of water. The view is free. A funicular, which is paid, saves the climb.
  • Porta Borsari and Castelvecchio. Back on the town side, a Roman gate of the first century still spans the main street. Beyond it stands the brick castle built by the della Scala in the 1350s. Its fortified bridge is free to cross.

The loop is about five kilometres and takes half a day without going inside anything.

The Scaliger tombs, seen from the street through their iron fence. Photo: Didier Descouens, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Ponte Pietra: Roman arches in pale stone, later ones in brick, all put back after 1945. Photo: Andrea Bertozzi, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Juliet's balcony

Shakespeare never saw Verona, and his lovers come from Italian stories written in the sixteenth century. The house in Via Cappello is a real medieval house that belonged to a family called Cappello, a name close enough to Capulet. The city bought it in 1905. The balcony was added in the 1930s, put together from old carved stone, and the bronze Juliet in the courtyard dates from 1972.

For years anyone could walk into the courtyard, and it was packed. That has ended: the city now lets visitors in by booked time slot, with one ticket for the courtyard alone and a fuller one that adds the rooms of the house. The scheme is recent and still being adjusted, so check how it works before you go.

What needs a ticket

  • The Arena, and now Juliet's courtyard and house.
  • The Torre dei Lamberti, the 84-metre tower above Piazza delle Erbe. A lift goes most of the way, or there are 368 steps. It gives the best view over the roofs.
  • The Castelvecchio Museum: medieval and Renaissance painting and sculpture from Verona, in rooms that the architect Carlo Scarpa remade from 1958.
  • The Roman Theatre and its archaeological museum, on the hillside beyond Ponte Pietra.
  • The four great churches: Sant'Anastasia, the cathedral, San Fermo, and San Zeno, a Romanesque basilica with bronze door panels and an altarpiece by Mantegna, twenty minutes' walk west of Castelvecchio. Each has a small ticket, and there is a combined one.

The city's visitor card, sold for one or two days, has long covered the Arena, the tower, the museums and the churches. It pays for itself if you go into three or more.

Piazza delle Erbe from the Lamberti tower: the square keeps the outline of the Roman forum. Photo: High Contrast, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0 DE.

Reading the partner's listings

  • The Arena fast track ticket is the one listing with entry. Its title says ticket. Its description speaks of meeting a local guide on Piazza Bra and going round with priority entry, and it gives no itemised list. Check which of the two you are buying, in what language and at what hour. It is a daytime visit, not a seat at the opera.
  • Three audio walks are commentary in the partner's app, on your own phone. All three say that tickets for the places on the way are not included.
  • They differ in route. One starts at Porta Nuova railway station and ends at Castelvecchio, which suits an arrival by train. One starts by Piazza Bra, crosses Ponte Pietra and ends on the hill of Castel San Pietro. The shortest, about an hour and a half, runs from Piazza delle Erbe to the cathedral.

These are the Arena ticket and the audio walks our partner sells in Verona, with today's prices:

[partner city="verona" match="verona" limit="4"]

The day in order

From Porta Nuova station it is a straight walk of about twenty minutes to Piazza Bra. Do the Arena first, before the groups and the heat. Walk the loop to Ponte Pietra before lunch. Keep the tower for the afternoon light and Castelvecchio for the end of the day. Museums in Verona have often opened late or not at all on Mondays: hours are on our pages for the Verona Arena and the Castelvecchio Museum.

From here

Lake Garda begins a quarter of an hour away by train, at Peschiera. Mantua is under an hour to the south, and Venice and Milan are each a little over an hour by fast train. See our page for the Torre dei Lamberti and the rest of Verona, or open the trip planner for Italy.

Cover photo: Elliott Brown, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

faqs.q: Is one day enough for Verona?
faqs.a: Yes. The old town fits inside a bend of the river, and a loop from the Arena to Ponte Pietra and Castelvecchio is about five kilometres. A day leaves time for the Arena, the tower and one museum.

faqs.q: Can you visit the Verona Arena during the day?
faqs.a: Yes, with a ticket: you walk the corridors and climb the stone tiers. During the opera season, from June to September, it closes to visitors early on performance days, so go in the morning.

faqs.q: What is free to see in Verona?
faqs.a: Piazza Bra, Piazza delle Erbe, Piazza dei Signori, the Scaliger tombs from the street, Ponte Pietra, the view from Castel San Pietro, Porta Borsari and the bridge of Castelvecchio.

faqs.q: Is Juliet's balcony in Verona real?
faqs.a: The house is medieval and belonged to a family called Cappello, but the balcony was added in the 1930s. Romeo and Juliet are characters from sixteenth-century Italian stories that Shakespeare reworked.

faqs.q: Where is the best view of Verona?
faqs.a: For the city in its loop of river, the free terrace of Castel San Pietro across Ponte Pietra. For the roofs and squares from the middle, the Torre dei Lamberti, which needs a ticket.

title: Ferrari and Lamborghini museums from Bologna: which is where, which ticket, and how to get there without a car
subtitle: Four museums in four towns, none of them in Bologna. What each one shows, which to pick, and the trains and buses that reach them.
excerpt: The two Ferrari museums are in Maranello and Modena, the two Lamborghini museums in Sant'Agata Bolognese and Funo. What each shows, which to choose, how to reach them from Bologna by train and bus, and how to read the partner's combined tickets.

featured_image.alt: A red 1950s Ferrari racing car with the number 8 on a white platform inside the Enzo Ferrari Museum in Modena

content_html:
[place attraction="museo-ferrari" city="bologna"]

Ferruccio Lamborghini made tractors. The son of farmers from Renazzo, in the plain north of Bologna, he started in 1948 by building them out of surplus military engines, and within ten years he was rich enough to buy Ferraris. He thought their clutches were weak. As he told the story in later life, he went to Maranello to say so to Enzo Ferrari, and was told that a man who built tractors should leave sports cars to those who understood them.

In 1963 Lamborghini opened a car factory of his own at Sant'Agata Bolognese, about thirty kilometres from Maranello. Three years later it showed the Miura. Whatever was really said that day, the result is on the map: four museums carrying the two names, in four different towns, with tickets sold singly, in pairs and all together. None of the four is in Bologna. Before you buy anything, sort out which is where.

Four museums, four towns

  • The Ferrari Museum, Maranello. Beside the factory, eighteen kilometres south of Modena. This is the racing one: Formula 1 cars from every decade, a hall of trophies, the road cars, and simulators that are paid for separately. The factory itself is not open to the public.
  • The Enzo Ferrari Museum, Modena. Ten minutes on foot from Modena railway station. It joins the house where Enzo Ferrari was born in 1898, with his father's workshop, to a hall of 2012 under a yellow aluminium roof shaped like the bonnet of a car. It is about the man and the early years, with a changing show of cars and a collection of engines.
  • The Lamborghini museum, Sant'Agata Bolognese. At the factory gate, about twenty-five kilometres north-west of Bologna. Two floors run from the first cars of the 1960s through the Miura and the Countach to the current models and a few one-offs.
  • The Ferruccio Lamborghini Museum, Funo. In a business district a dozen kilometres north of Bologna. It is the family's museum, set up by his son Tonino: tractors, Ferruccio's own cars, a prototype helicopter, a racing powerboat, his office put back together. It has often opened by reservation, so check before you go.

A Ferrari 125 S, the model of 1947 that was the first to carry the name. Photo: Christine und Hagen Graf, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

Which to choose

  • One museum, and you follow Formula 1: Maranello.
  • One museum, with the least travelling: the Enzo Ferrari Museum. Modena also has a Romanesque cathedral on the UNESCO list and a good lunch.
  • Both Ferrari museums: the natural pair, and a comfortable day. Ferrari sells a ticket for the two together.
  • Lamborghini cars: Sant'Agata.
  • The man behind them, and the tractors: Funo, which is quieter and stranger than the other three.
  • All four: two days without a car.

Allow an hour and a half to two hours in Maranello, and about an hour in each of the others.

A Miura in the museum at Sant'Agata Bolognese. Photo: Leonard J. DeFrancisci, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Getting there without a car

Modena and Maranello

Regional trains leave Bologna Centrale for Modena several times an hour and take twenty to thirty minutes. The Enzo Ferrari Museum is a short walk from the station. For Maranello there are two ways on: a public bus from Modena's bus station, which takes about half an hour and stops in the town, or the shuttle that has linked Modena station, the Enzo Ferrari Museum and the museum in Maranello. The shuttle is paid, runs only a few times a day and has not run in every season, so look at its timetable first. Check the time of the last ride back before you go into the museum.

Sant'Agata Bolognese

There is no railway. A regional bus from Bologna's bus station, a few minutes from the railway station, takes about an hour. It runs less often on Sundays and holidays. A taxi from Bologna is quick and costly.

Funo

Local trains on the line from Bologna to Ferrara stop at Funo in about ten minutes. From the station the museum is a walk of twenty minutes or more along roads built for lorries, or a short taxi ride.

Ferrari and Lamborghini on the same day

By public transport it means going back through Bologna or Modena between the two, and it works only with an early start and a taxi for at least one leg. With a hired car all four fit into one long day.

The hall of the Ferruccio Lamborghini Museum at Funo. Photo: TKOIII, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Reading the partner's listings

The partner files all of these under Bologna, although none is in the city. There are eight:

  • Four single entries: the Ferruccio Lamborghini Museum, the Lamborghini museum at Sant'Agata, the Enzo Ferrari Museum in Modena, and the Ferrari Museum in Maranello with a short session on a Formula 1 simulator.
  • Three pairs: Lamborghini at Sant'Agata with Ferrari in Maranello, Lamborghini at Sant'Agata with Enzo Ferrari in Modena, and the two Lamborghini museums together.
  • One ticket for all four, which its description says can be used over two days.

The titles are easy to mix up. "Lamborghini and Ferrari Museum" means Maranello. "Lamborghini Museum and Enzo Ferrari Museum" means Modena. Read the town in the description.

None of the eight gives an itemised list of what is included, and none mentions transport: assume you make your own way to each door. Some descriptions speak of the production lines at Sant'Agata. A factory visit there is a separate booking with limited places, so do not take it as part of a museum ticket unless the listing says so plainly. The partner has no ticket for the two Ferrari museums alone.

These are the Ferrari and Lamborghini museum tickets our partner sells, with today's prices:

[partner city="bologna" match="ferrari,lamborghini" limit="8"]

An early Lamborghini tractor. The tractors came fifteen years before the cars. Photo: Thomas Vogt, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

From here

In Modena, the cathedral, its leaning bell tower and the square in front of them are five minutes from the Enzo Ferrari Museum by bus, or twenty on foot. The makers of traditional balsamic vinegar in the countryside around receive visitors by appointment. Back in Bologna, the Ducati Museum at Borgo Panigale completes the set for anyone who prefers two wheels. See our pages for the Ferrari Museum and the Enzo Ferrari Museum, for Modena and Bologna, or open the attractions map of Italy.

Cover photo: Chris Olszewski, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

faqs.q: How do you get to the Ferrari museum from Bologna without a car?
faqs.a: Take a regional train from Bologna Centrale to Modena, twenty to thirty minutes. The Enzo Ferrari Museum is a short walk from the station. For Maranello, continue by public bus from Modena or by the museums' shuttle when it runs.

faqs.q: Which Ferrari museum is better, Maranello or Modena?
faqs.a: Maranello is the racing museum, with Formula 1 cars and trophies beside the factory. Modena is about Enzo Ferrari and the early years, and is far easier to reach by train. Fans of racing choose Maranello.

faqs.q: How do you get to the Lamborghini museum from Bologna by bus?
faqs.a: A regional bus from Bologna's bus station reaches Sant'Agata Bolognese in about an hour. There is no railway, and buses are fewer on Sundays and holidays.

faqs.q: Can you visit the Ferrari and Lamborghini museums in one day?
faqs.a: With a car, yes. By public transport it works only with an early start and a taxi for at least one leg, because you must go back through Bologna or Modena between them.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the two Lamborghini museums?
faqs.a: The museum at Sant'Agata Bolognese, at the factory, shows the cars from the 1960s to today. The Ferruccio Lamborghini Museum at Funo is the family's museum about the founder, with tractors, his own cars and a helicopter.
